subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise to a point of order concerning the amendment to the amendment moved on April 30, by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer). As Your Honour is aware an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) which appears at page 2445 of Hansard as follows:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade.
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect this end.
Then the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River is to be found at page 2676 of Hansard as follows:
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after "that" and substituting therefore the following:
This house regrets that there is no indication in the budget that the government intends to take any action to put an end to the unnecessary suffering of our people arising out of the policy of financial deflation, unwise and inequitable tariff policies and economies which inevitably lead to restrictions on the production and distribution of wealth. Such policies are responsible for the present condition of poverty in the midst of plenty.
And' further, that this house is of the opinion that the control of national credit, which by the constitution is vested in this parliament, should be exercised immediately by the government so as to:
Provide sufficient purchasing power to enable our people to "loosen their belts," and to take full advantage, as consumers, of their ability to produce;
Then follow four or five other paragraphs in the amendment to the amendment.
First of all I should like to draw the attention of the house to the votes and proceedings for January 31, 1934, when the following resolution was moved by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) and seconded by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer).
Whereas, the provision of an adequate medium of exchange through the issue and control of currency, is a fuction inherent in the state, and one which is wholly within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, and
Whereas, the transfer of this function to private interests to be used as a means of profit, rather than as a public service, has enabled those controlling finance to dominate every phase in the industrial and economic life of the nation, and
Whereas, the depressed and chaotic conditions which now prevail would indicate that this financial control, as at present exercised has proved itself detrimental to the best interests of the people of this country;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the reassumption of this responsibility, and the creation of a national system of credit and finance, to be controlled in the interests of all the people, and under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament.
I recall that upon that occasion the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) rose to a point of order, stating that the entire question had been referred in the present session to the standing committee on banking and commerce. He used the following words:
As we shall have to debate these matters later, why should we prolong this discussion in view of what has been said, when we know 74726-180
that when these bills reach this house they will be discussed, and when they reach the committee be discussed again at still greater length.
So, while I find myself to a very substantial degree in sympathy with the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River sitting to my left, I wish to raise this point of order: In the first place, in the amendment to the amendment I find these words: "suffering of our people arising out of the policy of financial deflation." That question has been specifically referred to the banking and commerce committee, as the result of a resolution by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).
In the second place there is a reference to "unwise and inequitable tariff policies." That question is covered in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth.
The remaining part of the amendment to the amendment deals with the question of national credit, and I submit that question is at the present time being discussed by the standing committee on banking and commerce. Inasmuch as the substance of the amendment to the amendment is now before the committee on banking and commerce, the only other reference in regard to "inequitable tariff policies" I submit is embraced in the mention of "genuine nationalism" in the amendment itself.
For these reasons I therefore submit that as a result of the deliberations of the committee on banking and commerce ample opportunities will be afforded to the house to discuss in every detail the questions of national credit, because that question has been definitely submitted to the banking and commerce committee. For those reasons I submit with all respect that the present amendment to the amendment is not in order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with my remarks I beg you to allow me to present to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in my name and that of the Liberal party in this house our most heartfelt sentiments of sympathy in his great bereavement. May the depth and sincerity of our feelings lighten to some extent, if possible, the sorrowfulness of his deep mourning.
When I adjourned the debate the other evening I was asking a question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I was going to ask him about the statement which he made in speaking on the budget on April 23, 1934, as reported at page 2446 of Hansard:
Personally I think that if gold is as necessary in the carrying on of our trade as everyone seems to imagine, the only permanent solution would be for the government to take over the gold mines. They could then keep the miners at work on a reasonable wage scale; they would then be able to collect this fortuitous gain instead of turning it over to private individuals.
The question I would ask my hon. friend is how is he going to proceed with the expropriation of our gold mines? I have studied very impartially the platform of the C.C.F. party and I observe that one of the main planks of their platform is the nationalization of our industries. But there are certain details of that policy of which it is only right that this house and the country should be seized, and especially when the leader of that party picks out a particular industry and says that he would nationalize it for certain reasons. What would be his procedure in nationalizing this particular industry? Would he nationalize only the mines that are on a dividend basis, or only those that are not paying their way at the present time or the whole of them.
He should also tell the house of the conflict that there might be between federal and provincial authorities if this question ever became an issue. The leader of the C.C.F. party must surely be aware of the fact that all the gold mines and for that matter all the mines of this country are primarily owned by the provinces, and that all the grants have been made and all the prospecting has been done or regulated by the provinces. What would 74726-1804
be the attitude of the provinces on the nationalization of the gold mines of this country? It is a well-known fact that more good money has been spent in promoting gold mines than has ever been made out of them. What would be the procedure of the leader of the C.C.F. party then? Would he have this country embark upon an enterprise in which in a great many cases there would be failure before it ever got started. That is one of the things which this house and the country at large has a right to know.
The hon. gentleman must also be aware of the fact that even with the high price of gold to-day only fifteen or sixteen mines in this country are on a paying basis. If his party were in office and he were in power would he propound the expropriation of the gold mines and the nationalization of the gold mining industry? What would be his procedure? What attitude would he take to the mine owner, and on what basis would he award compensation to the owner and shareholders? These are things which the people have a right to know when such a statement is made in this house by an hon. member occupying such a high position in his party. As I stated a few moments ago, I have studied from an impartial standpoint the policies and planks of the platform of the C.C.F. party and I believe that the hon. member owes it to himself and to parliament to state definitely what mode of procedure he would take in expropriating the gold mines.
Did the hon. member ever visualize, so far as gold mining is concerned-I am speaking of only that one industry-that practically everything that has been done in connection with our gold mines has been done on the personal initiative of the Canadian people, by prospectors and promoters and people who have developed these mines? Does the hon. member wish to create the impression that the government is more capable of running these mines than those who have had charge of them in the past? I would ask the hon. member to answer these questions on the next occasion when he speaks of this matter because, Mr. Speaker, this house and the country have a right to know what procedure the hon. member would adopt in respect to our gold mines, and if he is going to single out one particular industry, one part of our national life for nationalization, why not widen the scope of his policy and nationalize every single industry?
When I adjourned the debate on the budget the other evening I was speaking on the gold tax. I had said that I was in harmony with
previous speakers, even on the government

The Bridget-Mr. Bradette
ment the critical position, of the industry, I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite to consider the views that have been put forward 'by members of parliament as well as by other *people to show how absolutely unfair and onerous this tax is. The hon. member for Nelson pointed this out, and other members of parliament have urged the government to recognize the unfairness of this taxation on one industry.
The Prime Minister suggested that the agitation against this taxation was started iby the populace. Well, the sentiment of the people in this regard has been voiced by the newspapers, and the popular sentiment has been unanimous against this tax, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In other words, no one could help being familiar with the situation, so that the government had to give way. I want to be fair to the government, but I want the government to be sincere. I am sure that had they given this whole question that careful analysis which it deserved, instead of trying to raise $10,000,000 from one industry alone, had they studied the question of taxation a little further, their attitude would have been different. Suppose they had remained adamant in the application of this tax, what would have happened? As we pointed out, it would have meant the destruction of at least 80 per cent of the gold mining activities of Canada.
In this regard I should like to quote briefly from an editorial which has appeared in a newspaper sympathetic to this government, a weekly paper published in the Timmins district, and fully conversant with the whole subject and also sympathetic to the federal Minister of Mines.

Most people are aware of the fact that the dominion Minister of Mines, Hon. W. A. Gordon, and the Ontario Minister of Mines, Hon. Chas. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is with deep regret that I learned of the death of the wife of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), and as the first member on this side of the house to address you this afternoon, sir, I take this opportunity, on behalf of the members on this side as well as of myself, of extending our most sincere sympathy to him in his bereavement.
The hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), the official critic of the official opposition, in his address on this budget adopted an expedient which is not at all unfamiliar to lawyers, namely, the setting up of some straw men in order to knock them down. Hence, though it was no part of the budget at all, he endeavoured to set up the problem of bimetallism and a turnover tax because, I suggest, he lacked the ability to make a strong, sound and logical criticism of the proposals which were contained in that budget. He concluded that criticism by moving a resolution, and in that resolution he was indeed more definite than in his criticism, because we find in the resolution one condemnation of this government for what was alleged to be its policy. In amendment, he moved:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade.
For a few moments I wish to consider the question whether the policy of this government is one of economic nationalism. When this government came into power in 1930 the world was already in the sweep of a vast depression and unemployment was rife not only in other countries but in Canada as well. In every country in the world there was a vast surplus of production of which it was desirous to dispose; and shortly before this government came into power Italy, the United States, France, Germany and other countries had increased their tariffs, so that Canada could not sell her exportable surplus in any of those markets. Each of these countries in turn had large exportable surpluses which they wished to sell in any market in the world, which they were willing to sell, not at prices representative of cost of production, but at

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
any price which could be obtained. The result was that Canada at that time was a fair field in which they might dump their surplus products.
Faced with these conditions this government did immediately increase its tariff and it increased the tariff not, as our opponents would desire to lead the electorate to believe, for the purpose of developing trade but for the purpose of using that tariff as a defensive instrument in the protection of Canada. Now, having taken a defensive measure, this government set about negotiating trade treaties in order that our trade might be increased. Treaties were negotiated with the component parts of the British Empire, and also with Austria, France and, if my recollection serves me rightly, with Germany. As a result of those treaties Canada has increased her trade and also the amount of employment. It is all very well for the hon. member for Shel-bume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) to compare Canada's trade in 1929 with her trade in 1933, but I suggest that a fairer comparison would be to compare Canada's trade in 1929 with world trade in 1929 and to compare Canada's trade in 1933 with world trade in 1933. If we make the comparison on that basis, this is what we find: World trade in 1929 amounted to $68,641,000,000 while in 1933 the world trade estimated, as the figures for all countries are not quite complete, is $22,000,000,000. In other words, world trade dropped 68 per cent between 1929 and 1933. If we turn to our great neighbour to the south we find that their total trade in 1929 was around $9,500,000,000 while in 1933 it was $3,381,000,000, or a drop of 65 per cent. If we take Canada's trade for the year 1929 we find that it was about $2,481,000,000 while in 1933 it amounted to $932,963,000, or a drop of only 62 per cent.
If during a period when world trade dropped 68 per cent and when the trade of our neighbour dropped 65 per cent, Canada's trade dropped only 62 per cent and if economic nationalism, so-called, is the cause of that favourable position for Canada, then I am in favour of that policy of economic nationalism. If when you add to that the fact that since 1933 Canada under the policies of this government has advanced from the position of a nation with an adverse balance of trade in excess of $100,000,000 to that of a nation with a favourable balance of trade in excess of $100,000,000, I say again that if that be economic nationalism, then I favour economic nationalism.
The hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette), who preceded -me, spoke of the gold tax. His utterances in many instances were extreme. He reminded me of some of the hysteria that was published in some Canadian papers in connection with the gold tax. I only trust that in the next election all Liberal members on the opposite side of the house will invite the hon. member for North Timiskaming into their constituencies to tell the people that he and the party which he supports favoured the tax on sugar-

speechtext:
Such an outburst only stimulates any tendency there might have been on the part of shareholders to liquidate their stock with losses to the selling shareholders. It is indeed with strange inconsistency that while the Northern Miner was roundly condemning this government for the great injury it was doing to the gold mining industry of this country, that same paper was carrying the most glowing advertisements for the sale of shares in gold mining companies, one of them in particular advising the public that gold shares had indeed "very attractive possibilities." One caption especially caught my eye; it said:
"How shareholders will be hit." "Dividend cuts coming."
If you then read -the article you would find that it went on to tell how Hollinger, one of the gold -mines, would lose an amount equal to seven of its periodical five-cent dividends and so would its shareholders. Let
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

us examine the situation in respect to that very mine. Hollinger has been in the habit for years of paying a dividend of five cents a month per share with a bonus of five cents a share in the twelfth month, or alternatively a dividend equal to five cents per share every four weeks. The public were led to believe that by the imposition of this tax seven of those dividends in succession would be cut off. What are the facts? In 1933 the Hollinger mine produced 481,279 ounces of gold and they sold that gold at an average price of $28.60 an ounce. Let me assume that in the year 1934 the number of ounces produced is the same. The price for gold having now advanced to $35 an ounce, they would sell every ounce of it, even after deducting the tax as originally proposed, at $31.50 an ounce, or after deducting the tax as now amended, at $31.42 an ounce. In view of prices this year, the same production would return to the Hollinger mine, after deduction of the tax, an extra $1,395,000. This would increase the earning of that mine from $1.16 to $1.45 a share or, in other words, a difference of twenty-nine cents a share. Therefore, instead of this tax having the effect of cutting off seven consecutive dividends from the shareholders of the Hollinger mines the truth is that with the same production that mine will be able to pay six more consecutive dividends of five cents per share in the year 1934. If you make a similar calculation in respect to the production of the Lake Shore mine, at the end of 1934, even after paying its tax, that mine should have an additional amount of seventy-two cents per share to distribute among its shareholders.
Under the amendment some exemption is made for low grade producers. Some of the wildest and most extravagant statements have been made with respect to the effect on low grade producers; a circular I have before me, issued by one brokerage house, says one hundred thousand men will be put out of work. If I understood the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) correctly, I think he put the figure at eighty thousand.

Then I withdraw the statement; I thought I understood the hon. gentleman to say that this measure would cause unemployment in the mines affecting about eighty thousand men. I say this, sir: I challenge anyone to give concrete evidence proving that, even had the tax remained on low

grade producers, it would have put one-half of one hundred thousand or one-quarter of one hundred thousand men out of work in this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, if you please; I did not interrupt you. I have an argument I wish to make. I am not so sure, Mr. Speaker, that it is economically sound to help these low grade producers, so called, to continue to endeavour to get into production unless they have a reasonable expectancy of ore that will enable them to operate profitably at $26 an ounce for gold at least, if not at $20.67. What was the reason for the advance in the price of gold? If I understand it correctly it was because certain nations of the world accepted, temporarily at least, an economic theory,- that theory being that if you increased the price of gold you deflated or devalued your currency based on gold, and that in turn if you devalued your currency you increased the prices of commodities.
The acceptance of that economic theory,-[DOT] plus another theory so far as the United States was concerned,-caused that country and some other nations of the world to increase the price of gold. If that economic theory is sound obviously when we get back to the days of prosperity the price of gold should be reduced by every country of the world, presumably by Canada as well. At that rate, sir, as soon as we get back to prosperity, down will go the price of gold and then, I ask, what will become of the shareholders who have been induced, by promoters desirous of selling stocks, to invest their money in low grade producers that cannot possibly exist except upon a very much enhanced value for gold? In view of that situation, sir, I am not at all convinced that it is economically sound to encourage these low grade producers to greater production, but out of consideration for the shareholders who have been induced to invest their money in them I support the amendment suggested by the Prime Minister in connection with the low grade producers.
Now, sir, I wish to deal with another aspect of this amendment. After declaring this government guilty of economic nationalism the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) proceeds:
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit-

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
I must confess, sir, that I am a little at a loss to know just what the other policies respecting credit may be, unless the utterance of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) to-day, in which he informed our friends in the far corner that he was in sympathy with the provisions of their amendment to the amendment, indicates that the old Liberal party is trying now somehow to crawl on the bandwaggon of inflation.

speechtext: You are on it now; $35,000,000 last year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is quite apparent from the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that his idea of inflation and mine vary widely, but I will come to that in a moment. In considering the progress Canada has made under this government I think sometimes it is well to ascertain what is 'being said by people not resident in Canada, who cannot be accused of having a biased mind. A short time ago I noticed an article in the Saturday Evening Post by Mr. Isaac F. Mar-cosson. In comparing Canada's progress with that of our great neighbour to the south Mr. Marcosson said:
-the index of the physical volume of Canadian business-the economic pulse of the nation -advanced by thirty-two per cent between February and November, 1933 that industrial production increased forty-three per cent in the same period-that purchasing power is up twelve per cent-
If this resolution, so far as it relates to some new credit system, involved what I anticipate it does, having regard to some of the speeches that have been made in this house, I should like to offer some views with respect thereto. Inflation, as I understand it, means the issuing of new money beyond the metal coverage now required by the Canadian statute or formerly required by international practice, and the use and distribution of that money by payment for public services. If we embark upon any vast scheme of the distribution of currency in excess of that which is available, of necessity we must print money without reference to metal coverage as a controlling factor or base, and if you do that I say you have uncontrolled inflation. Can inflation be controlled? In my opinion it can be controlled only in one of two ways. It can never be controlled by the agency of government so long as it may be affected by the whim of government. In my opinion it can be controlled only by a metal coverage or base internationally recognized or by t'he setting up of a sinking fund into which annually an amount of money raised by taxation is poured for the purpose of meeting the issued currency upon demand and at
likely maturity. Inflation, Mr. Speaker, has been the last desperate effort of nearly all countries in distress; they have seized it as a drowning man grasps at a straw, but it has never saved any nation that has tried1 it. It has ruined commercially and economically every nation in the world that has been seduced by its charm.
I am one of those who admit that the present monetary unit, which is expressed in dollars, varies in purchasing power in relation to the value of commodities. I will admit, further, that in my opinion any monetary unit that varies in its relative value to prices of other commodities imposes in times of depression a burden upon debtors. An ideal monetary system would be one in which the monetary unit always held comparatively the same relative value to commodities. But the wit of man has not as yet devised such a monetary unit, and in this House of Commons I have not heard one suggested which in my opinion has those qualifications. I will further admit that I would be in favour of a reflationary policy if you could reflate and still have your reflation under control. But as I previously outlined I do not believe it can be controlled, except by the two methods I indicated. And the moment, sir, that you endeavour to put into effect any policy of inflation or reflation which is not automatically controlled, then I suggest you are getting away from the principle of sound money.
I have deliberately used the term "sound" in reference to money. I have used it because so much has been said about "sound" money. Some hon. member in this house has said that sound money is wholly unsound. What is sound money? Money is not like flowers, plants or animals of which one may have several species. There are only two kinds of money, sound and unsound. There is safe money and there is unsafe money. In my opinion sound money is safe money. One of my colleagues, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) stated in this House of Commons that sound money has been sweet sounding for the receivers of interest, but that it has meant fury to the masses of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, with that statement I absolutely disagree. If sound money is safe money, then in my opinion it is sweet sounding to every man and woman in Canada who is in receipt of a fixed income, irrespective of Whether that income be by way of wages, by way of dividends, by way of interest or by way of profits. Sound money to my mind should be sweet sounding to every wage earner in Canada. Sound money should be sweet sounding to every man in this country in receipt of a pension.
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

Sound money should be sweet sounding to every woman in Canada who is in receipt of a mother's allowance to help maintain herself and her children. Sound money should be sweet sounding to every aged person unable longer to work, and who is in receipt of an old age pension. Sound money, sir should be sweet sounding to every person in Canada who is in receipt of a fixed income, because that person knows that when he is in receipt of one of those sound dollars he can exchange it for a very reasonable quantity of other commodities, and that he will not have to have a thousand of those dollars to exchange for a loaf of bread.
Considerable has been said about the policy adopted by our great neighbour to the south. It has been stated that they have done very well through a policy of inflation, and that the steps they have taken constitute an inflation policy. That I cannot see. If I have appreciated it correctly, the Roosevelt policy in the United States has introduced into the monetary system two new principles. The first is the nationalization of gold and the second is the revaluation of gold. Neither of those steps amounts to inflation. The United States has about seven billion dollars in gold. On the presently accepted international standard of metal coverage of 25 per cent they could have currency in circulation up to twenty-eight billions of dollars. The fact is that the United States has not one-half of twenty-eight billions of dollars in currency circulation. I ask hon. members this question: How can you have a green back with a gold backing? In resolutions which have been discussed we have heard a great deal about the policy of this government being deflationary, about the value of the dollars being increased and thereby pressing down the prices of commodities. But surely, sir, the record of the relative value of our currency to those of other countries is a complete answer to that allegation. Let me point out that when the United States was on a gold dollar basis, the basis which formerly was internationally recognized, the highest average premium at which their currency ever stood was of 17 per cent. For a few days it did touch 21 per cent, but the average stood at 17 per cent. To-day we have had the government of that country tell us that the American dollar is worth only 59-4 per cent of what it was when it was the so-called gold dollar. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the difference in its value should be about 40 per cent. If their money was at a premium of 17 per cent over ours at a time when they had a gold dollar, and it is now worth 40 per cent or 40 cents less, then to-

day the Canadian dollar should be at a premium of 23 per cent, if this government in turn had not been alive to the movements of the times, and if this government had been carrying out a policy of deflation of our dollar.
Then the suggestion is made in this house that arbitrarily we should cut interest rates. One hon. member has suggested that we should pass a statute whereby the interest rates on all our bonds should be cut by one-third, that the rates on bonds of corporations in Canada should be cut by the same amount, and that at the tail end of that statute we should have a provision whereby such changes would not come into effect until the government passed an order in council. Then, armed with this blunt instrument of a statute of repudiation to be propelled by the force of an order in council the Canadian people would go forth into foreign lands to wage economic war. Well, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what success we would have under such a system. Repudiation-and I say this in all kindness to the gentleman who advocated it -is to my mind nothing but a stupid remedy for a primitive nation. Gullible indeed would be the man who would lend money to this country unless he believed that the bargain for repayment would be carried out. Yet it is suggested that we should go to our bondholders outside this country and say to them, "If you do not accept bonds from us with your interest rate cut one-third, then we will pass this order in council." What chance do you think we would ever have to borrow money again from those people? Do you think they would accept our story, at a time when we might go back into a foreign market to get more money which is so necessary for the development of this country, if we said, "Well, we were bad little boys. True, we repudiated once, but if you will just lend us some money again we will be good little boys and never repudiate again." What a nice position for Canada.
Let me consider it from the standpoint of our domestic situation. Most of the advocacy of repudiation of our interest rates is espoused by those who go throughout this country and endeavour to paint a picture of vast corporations that have made enormous profits by grinding down the ordinary man, commonly called the poor; but let us see what we would do to these vast corporations if we should pass this statute of repudiation. The private corporations of this country have payable in this year 1934, $132,563,994, of which $115,278,081 is interest. So if we pass this statute of repudiation the first people

The Budget-Mr. Reid
on whom we will confer a benefit will be these vast corporations, and to the extent of one-third of their interest of $115,000,000 odd, or something like a benefit of $41,000,000. That would hardly put much benefit into the hands of the individual holders who have invested their money in the bonds of these corporations. I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that if I were to be governed solely by the emotions of my heart, and not by the thoughts of my head, I might at times be inclined to favour a measure of repudiation especially when I go about the riding I represent and see the deprivation and want among many of the people. I am reminded that a great divine, I think it was Henry Ward Beecher, once wrote, "Where you find religion of the heart you have a fanatic. Where you find religion of the head you have a heretic. Where you find religion which is a combination of heart and head you have a Christian." I believe, sir, that if we are going to solve the problems of this country we must use our heads, as well as our hearts, and the solution in my opinion never will lie in repudiation.
May I ask one question: What man has ever improved his standing in his own community, even among his fellow-debtors, by repudiation? Not one. Now this nation is nothing but an aggregate of the individuals in this country, and just as no man can improve his standing in his own community by repudiation, neither can this nation, by repudiation, improve its standing among the nations of the world.
Something has been said as to why Canada has not adopted the policies in economic matters which have been adopted by the United States. Well, in the first place, sir, it must be realized that in international affairs Canada is not a pivotal nation. Unlike the United States, we are a debtor, not a creditor, nation. Unlike the United States, we have very little more gold than is required under the former international standard to back our currency. If, instead of shipping out of this country vast quantities of gold as was done by the Minister of Finance in the former Liberal government in 1927, 1928 and 1929, to meet our unfavourable trade balances of those years, we had been able to hold that gold in this country, I am sure that we could have gratified the desires even of our friends in the extreme comer by the additional amount of currency that could have been issued as safe and sound money. But Canada not being a pivotal nation in international affairs, being as we are affected to a large
extent by conditions in the United States, being also affected as we are by conditions in the United Kingdom, we must at all times maintain our dollar within reasonable limits of the American dollar and the British pound sterling. Consequently, we have been very much in the position of a boy who sits in the middle of a teeter-totter. We have not had the pleasure, by enacting new monetary measures, of bobbing up and down on either end and obtaining that thrill, but nevertheless we have had a much more stable position, and when the game is over we are much more likely to have a settled stomach. Now in view of the fact that we must maintain the value of our currency relative to that of the United States and the United Kingdom it cannot be fixed by this government until some relative value is attained between the American dollar and the pound sterling.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe that those who are shrewd observers will agree that in the first few years after confederation a great Conservative leader, Sir John A. Macdonald, made Canada, and history I think will record, that in the last few years of depression a masterful leader of the Conservative party, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, saved Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the budget I would first of all like to join with others in expressing my regrets at the sudden loss sustained by the 'hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). I believe most members will agree with me that he is one of the best liked ministers in the house.
Within the limited time at my disposal it will not be possible for me to deal with all the matters brought down in the budget, and dealt with in the budget speech of the Finance minister, but before proceeding to deal with some of the points may I refer to a statement that was made in the debate by the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Shaver) who a few days ago twitted me with advocating that white Canadian seamen be employed on the ships subsidized by this country, and also advocating a reduction in freight rates, while not agreeing with the policies advocated by this government. I have not the time at my disposal to go into that, Mr. Speaker, except to say that I can see no relation whatever between the proposals that I put before the house in regard to white seamen being employed, the question of freight rates, and not supporting the policies of this government under which the textile companies in this country have received

speechtext: The bonds of the Canadian National Railways; like other bonds of the Dominion of Canada, are held to a large extent by various investors in the United States. About three-quarters of the bonds are held in the United States by insurance companies, banks and individuals.

speechtext:
But like our own railways, they have certain investments. Our own railways have investments in United States railroads, and, likewise, United States railroads have placed their funds in other investments.
I should like to refer for a few moments to another serious matter confronting the country, that of unemployment which has been steadily increasing since 1930. According to the official figures brought down in the house not long ago, in January, 1931, the total unemployed amounted to 132i,000; this figure had increased to 355,806 in 1932; to 1,244,536 in
1933.	The figures Showed a slight decrease in
1934.	there being 1,228,246 individuals receiving relief. I am not one of those who believe that unemployment as we know it to-day is something which will not be with us always. Machinery has displaced men to such a degree during the past twenty-five years that the great masses of our people can never hope to be engaged in industry. Until our government recognizes that unemployment is permanent I do not believe we will arrive at any solution of the matter. One of the most serious aspects of this matter is the question of our youth. I was surprised to learn that there are some 600,000 youths in Canada between the ages of nineteen and twenty-five. The greater proportion of these young people have no great outlook in life and I believe that most of them are to-day in idleness. To my mind that is one of the most serious aspects of the matter. We sometimes say that this is a war on unemployment. We spent in the last war many millions of dollars destroying life and surely it is not too much to expect that we could spend a great deal more to save life, in this one I think that is something well worth considering, especially from the point of view of saving the youth of the country.
I wish now to speak for a few moments regarding the debts of Canada. Every hon. member must be aware of the great burden of debt which is hanging over this country. When one realizes that the total value of our agricultural wealth for the last year was not sufficient to pay the interest charges in Canada, it is very striking indeed; and when we have reached the point where we are borrowing many millions to pay interest charges -not principal but interest charges-one must ask oneself-When will the end of this be? Personally I believe our debts will never be paid, and the sooner we realize that the better. I listened a few moments ago to the hon. member for West York who spoke about repudiation. It is no repudiation to call in those to whom you owe money and make a plain statement of the state of affairs in the country. I am not unmindful of what transpired in a country like Great Britain. After telling the people to tighten their belts she did not stop there altogether, but in good fashion went after the bondholders. In 1931 Viscount Snowden warned the country of the grave danger facing it, and after he had warned the people from his place in the House of Lords, the nation took stock and set to work to retrieve its position. Among other things it is interesting to know that Great Britain converted $10,000,000,000, more than the total debt of Canada, from a 5 per cent issue down to a 3-i per cent; yet we have hon. members in this house talking about repudiation if anyone gets up and suggests cutting the interest rate.
In my opinion the people are tired of being told to tighten their belts until such time as the bondholders and others are gone after. It surely is not repudiation if you call in the people who own the bonds and notify them that you can no longer pay because it is sapping the life blood of the country, and say to them, "We are either willing to give you your money back or give you 3| per cent." If something of that kind is not done I am afraid the whole thing will be wiped out and they will be in danger of losing all.
I have not the time to go as far as I should like with regard to the debt situation because in most of my remarks I wish to deal with trade. But I believe that we should adopt the policies that have been adopted in at least eight or ten countries which, in setting their houses in order, have practically told bondholders that they will have to accept less. If we are to follow the example of any country, surely it is not amiss to suggest that we should emulate a country like Great Britain where, it is well to note, the bond-
The Budget-Mr. Reid

holders, in good spirit, agreed to accept 3i per cent. So that I cannot agree with my hon. friend when he talks about repudiation. Repudiation means wiping the whole slate clean and calling the debt off, and I am one of those who does not accept that suggestion. I do maintain however that the common citizens of the country are tired of being told to tighten their belts, because if some of them tighten their belts much more, both parts of the belt might meet. Many have been tightening their belts for the last three or four years and are now of the opinion that others who have not borne the brunt should come forward and show their true citizenship by agreeing at this time to accept a much lower rate of interest.
