I am inclined to think that this subject having been brought to light in the manner in which it has is probably a good thing for the country and for the mining industry because it makes it possible for those who are interested in it and who perhaps know something about it to put before the public what the actual situation is. When you speak to men who are looking only at the returns from a few large mines they always refer to Lake Shore and Harry Oakes and Hollinger and Noah Timmins and these men. They lose sight altogether of the weeks and months and years that these men tramped the trails of northern Ontario in the effort to find these mines. And what they lose sight of to a greater degree is the fact that, as my hon. friend from North Timiskaming (Mr. Brad-ette) said to-day, for every dollar that has so far been taken out of the claims in this country a dollar and a half or two dollars has gone into the ground in the effort to find gold. I cannot give a better illustration than to read something that appeared in day before yesterday's issue of Saturday Night, in reference to one gold mine in northern Ontario:
Kirkland Lake has never paid a dividend, although having carried work to 5,500 feet in depth. This is pointed to in mining circles as evidence of the great courage displayed by those who finance mining enterprises, and as an illustration of why the shareholders of mining companies should not be taxed unduly at such times as they have the good fortune to back a winner. It is twenty years since the representative of Saturday Night first went over the McKane claims, then the nucleus of the Kirkland Lake mine-two decades of patient waiting by a courageous band of shareholders.
And yet those men under competent engineers, backed by the advice of the best geologists we have in this country-and we have some of the best in the world-aire going down, down and down, spending their own
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson

money, supported by their conviction that ultimately they will get gold in substantial, paying values.
Just one further illustration, because my time is limited. I have watched for four consecutive years the development of a gold area or what it is hoped will be a gold area. In 1928 a group of men, ready to venture all the money they themselves had in the world and their own time as well, started out on a prospecting campaign; they staked many claims and spent a tremendous amount of money, but in 1930 their prospectors came across a field that looked so promising that they staked some claims and began to work. For four long years not only that group but another group of men, with very substantial sums of money put into the enterprise by Canadian investors who were willing to stake claims, first, in the hope of getting some gold for themselves and, second, in their anxiety to develop this country, worked first on the surface, then by diamond drilling and later by sinking shafts. One of those properties is to-day so far developed that if you go down five hundred feet in shaft number one, travel through all the underground workings walking as rapidly as you can, and come out at shaft number two, 1,850 feet away, on the surface, it will take you four hours to do the walking. Yet, if you asked them to-day they would say that they do not know so far whether they have a mine, but to back up their efforts they have the conviction that something worth [DOT]while will ultimately be found. That is just a single illustration of what is taking place over all this great country.
May I repeat that this gold tax as ultimately placed is fair and equitable and is felt so to be by those in the best position to know; yet the general policy of this country should be to do everything possible to encourage and not to discourage new ventures in gold mining, because it will ultimately become the greatest asset this country has.
Just a word in conclusion. Beginning with the middle of last year, a consistent, constant, gradual improvement in business has been, generally speaking, going on across Canada. More men are being employed; more goods are moving; railway traffic is increasing and everything indicates a general rise, the best kind of rise that we can have. I am not for a moment going to suggest that we are by any means out of the woods; we have ahead of us difficulties, external and internal. My opinion is that the greatest shadow that overhangs the continued improvement of business in this country comes

from outside the dominion altogether, from what may happen in other countries. But we still have internal problems, the first and greatest of which is perhaps our debts, debts of every character, personal, corporate, municipal, provincial and federal, debts created first during the war period and then in the inflationary period following the war. By care, by sound thinking, we can get out of these debt difficulties. We cannot get out of them by the application of any patent formula. I am in the timber business; I have been taking out pulpwood this very year to manufacture paper, but you cannot get out of the difficulty by setting paper mills at work making paper and printing presses to print money on that paper; that is utterly impossible. It can be done only by hard work and the application of sound business principles. Regardless of what anybody else may say, that is my conviction. You might as well expect that a man could take his whole life's savings, whatever they might 'be, his house, clothes and everything else 'he has and make a bonfire of them and then feel he was going to be as materially well off as before, as to expect that this world can get away from the destruction of the period from 1914 to 1918 and the inflationary gambling period from 1921 to 1930 without having to work hard in order to climb the hill. What we require in Canada is patience, cooperation, in order to do that, and if we exercise those traits, we shall do it.
Another important problem and one that must give serious minded mem everywhere food for thought is that of our great' central west. The three prairie provinces-I am speaking as an outsider looking in but as one who has traversed them more than once- built up their material and social life principally around one great product, wheat. In the last five years the aspect of the wheat marketing possibilities has completely changed. Wheat is being grown in almost every country in the temperate zone, and European countries, where our great market formerly was, have in many cases practically closed their doors against us and are growing their own wheat. We cannot overcome that situation until they are ready to open these doors. Following that, perhaps the greatest difficulty is the menace of drought and insects in large parts of western Canada. For four years in succession a large section of that great area has been overtaken by drought. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth will blame the government for that, and maybe it is responsible; perhaps through the omnipotence with which it is credited, it could have overcome that but did not. This

The Budget-Mr. Hurtubise
year, if reports are correct, there is just as great a menace in the insect pests. My final word is this, that the condition of the central western provinces is a challenge to every right thinking man in this country. Some solution for these problems must be worked out, and they must. be worked out not by factious quarrelling as to methods and particular aspects of the matter but by cooperative effort on the part of all the Canadian people. If we apply ourselves in that way we shall ultimately succeed, overcome our difficulties and make Canada what we hope and always have hoped its destiny should be.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to join the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) in offering my heartfelt sympathy to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in his great bereavement.
It is not my intention to deal at length with the financial situation at present under discussion. Others have already brought forth many arguments which are of a constructive nature but which will be considered by some to be of a destructive nature. I believe in frank discussion where everyone can express his opinion, because something good and practical always comes out of it. It is from this point of view that I appreciate the privilege of saying a few words with regard to some matters that I have particularly at heart.
First, I want to join the hon. member who preceded me in congratulating the Minister of Finance on the noble effort he has made to frame a balanced budget and to convince the Canadian people that the depression is a thing of the past. I have a great deal of sympathy for the Minister of Finance; I know he has been working under great difficulties, but in my humble opinion he never will be able to balance his budget by only reducing his expenditures and imposing new taxes. Our national debt, including federal, provincial and municipal debts, has reached such a height that we cannot expect to meet our obligations and reduce our debts unless we adopt some radical means. The figures in regard to our national debt are as follows:
1930		 $2,177,763,959
1931		 2,261,611,937
1932		 2,375.346,172
1933		 2.599,089,000
1934		 2,789,152,000
In four years, therefore, we had an increase in our national debt of $596,000,000, and the debts of the provincial governments have increased in proportion. The gross debenture 74726-1S2
debt of municipalities of over 4.200, by provinces, as of December 31, 1931, was as follows:
Alberta	$	78,679,570
British Columbia	 129,913,890
Manitoba	 116,864,937
Ontario	 499,002,074
Nova Scotia	 31,386,025
New Brunswick	 21,477,521
Prince Edward Island.. ..	1,863,211
Quebec	 362,132,334
Saskatchewan	 47,488,595

Other liabilities, consisting of temporary loans, overdrafts on banks, accounts payable and so on, amount to $295,223,318. Interest payments on municipal bonded debts total about $63,000,000. While the figures for public debt can be obtained with approximate completeness, those having to do with private indebtedness can cover the field only partially. Out of a total of 654,297 owned and partly owned farms in the dominion, 244,201 were mortgaged to the extent of $677,564,100, and it should be pointed out that this figure refers only to the debt secured by mortgage or an equivalent legal instrument, on lands and buildings, and these figures include owned farms. It is estimated that the urban mortgages held by corporate lenders amount to about $765,000,000. Some estimate the general national debt at ten billion dollars, while others place it at twelve billion dollars.
This is a very discouraging situation, and I regret to be obliged to present such a dismal picture of conditions, but are we to sit content and listen to optimistic speeches while we refuse to heed the alarms that are being sounded to show that we are heading for disaster? In the last few years we have been advised by great authorities in economics that unless some radical change is made our social and economic system is doomed. We are crushed by debts, and just here I should like to quote a humorous article published two years ago which expresses very well the situation in which the people find themselves to-day. A man was asked to make a payment on his note, and here is his reply:
In reply to_ your recent requests to send you a cheque, I wish to inform you that the present shattered condition of my bank account makes it impossible for me to take your requests seriously.
My present financial condition is due to the effect of dominion laws, provincial laws, municipal laws, country laws, corporation laws, liquor laws, traffic laws, by-laws, brother-inlaws, sister-in-laws, mother-in-laws and outlaws, all of which have been foisted' upon an unsuspecting public.

The Budget-Mr. Hurtubise

Through these laws I am compelled to pay a business tax, sales tax, amusement tax, gas tax, school tax, water tax, excess tax, auto tax, hydro tax and syn-tax.
In addition to these irritating taxes I am forced by the strong arm of the law to get a permit for this thing and a permit for that thing. I am required to get a business licence, a city licence, a provincial licence, a sign licence, a dog licence, a motor licence, a radio licence, a liquor licence-not to mention my marriage licence.
I am also requested and required to contribute to every society and organization which the inventive genius of man is capable of bringing into life.
For my own safety, I am required to carry life insurance, liability insurance, fire insurance, compensation insurance, accident insurance, collision insurance, rain insurance, hail insurance and business insurance.
The government has now so governed my business that it is no easy matter for me to find out whq owns it. I am inspected, expected, introspected, suspected, disrespected, examined, reexamined, informed, required, summoned, fined, commanded and compelled, and simply because I refused to donate to each and all, and to go out and beg or borrow or steal money to give away, I am cussed, discussed, boycotted, talked to, talked about, lied to, lied about, held up, held down and robbed until I am nearly ruined.
This is a picture of the Canadian taxpayer to-day, and I do not know how long he will last. I have listened to three budget speeches; each time I was led to expect that at least we would balance our budget, but at the end of each fiscal year we had to face increasing deficits. I do not believe we will ever succeed in paying our debts so long as we have to borrow money to pay interest. We are in a queer situation; we all want prosperity, yet we have nothing but poverty; we want peace, but we have unrest. Since 1930 all kinds of palliatives have been tried in an attempt to cure the situation. All conceivable powers were given the government to cope with the difficulties confronting the country, but what did the people get under the unemployment relief acts in comparison with what they were promised so emphatically in 1930? They were given temporary relief and palliatives which to date have cost this country $112,000,000. We were all in favour of some kind of relief, and if at any session we opposed the relief act it was because the blank cheque was contrary to the principle of responsible government and to the control of parliament over legislation and expenditures. For the same reason we have opposed other legislations. In 1931 a program of public works was begun, but in 1932 and 1933 that program was replaced by a system of direct relief or dole which has been the curse of the country, even to the Tory party. Then, in 1934, on the eve of an election, we

are advised that a great construction program is to be started. We are told to cany on in the expectation that general conditions will improve and that matters will in time adjust themselves. In the meantime, however, the great mass of unemployed, the small town proprietors and the farmers are in a sad predicament. Many of them are being dispossessed. All have been waiting for the solution promised by the government and a great many are now so utterly discouraged that they do not care what the outcome may be. The panaceas advocated and adopted have proved to be altogether inadequate. Protection and high tariff are now repudiated by all economists, bankers and even by prominent Tory politicians. The intraempire trade is far from bringing the results which were expected. On the eve of an election the government has instituted a committee to investigate price spreads and mass buying. I would not be surprised if it were followed by the same effects which have followed other investigations. The Canadian people are anxiously watching these dillydallying operations and they are asking themselves if a remedy is going to be offered for the situation which is dragging us down to disaster. We must realize we are passing through a period of evolution. There are signs everywhere that the structure of national and international finance has permanently broken down and cannot be reconstructed along old lines. The government is doing little or nothing to cope with that situation.
Science and mechanization have made such progress that the whole economic system has been thrown out of balance. Agriculture, which has always been the basic fabric of our economic welfare, which has kept our capital active and has provided employment for the greater part of our population, has given place to science and to machinery. The use of machinery has displaced human labour and brought about the centralization of capital followed by unemployment and the freezing up of capital. On the other hand our assets have not diminished; they are the same as they were. Our means of production have increased and, as has been said, we are starving in the midst of plenty.
I believe the time has come when the government should consider drastic legislation for the reduction of our capital obligations and for the alleviation of the mortgage burden carried by the farmers and labourers who are making every effort to save their homes. Under the policies followed by the present government we will have some day to face one of three things: First, a substantial reduction in or

The Budget-Mr. Hurtubise
total suspension of all interest and compound interest on our capital debt, whether we like it or not; second,-and this is the course which most of us fear-the reduction or cancellation of part of certain capital debts, or, third, liquidation in the near future. I may be considered a pessimist, but when I make these statements I merely repeat what has been said by many national and international authorities in economics.
Following these general considerations I wish to refer to the budget speech. First may I direct my observations to the ten per cent tax which originally was imposed on the gross gold production. Some short time ago a change in that proposal, which will be much more acceptable to the country generally, was communicated to the house. The ten per cent tax on gross production would have been quite unjustifiable; it would have meant the closing down of many mines, and a death blow to prospectors who have made discoveries which have been the pride of the different provinces, and chiefly the province of Ontario. It would have meant unemployment for thousands of people either directly connected with or indirectly affected by mining.
Very shortly after the budget was published I received telegrams and letters from boards of trade in different cities and towns. I refer particularly to Sudbury and North Bay where there was a keen realization of the far- reaching effects of such a tax. The day following the delivery of the budget I received the following communication from the Sudbury board of trade:
Sudbury board of trade strongly protests the tax budget speech proposes placing upon gold production which will mean extinction of many small and low- grade producers now under development with consequent serious loss of employment in mines and in industrial and mercantile establishments catering to the industry.
Then, the board of trade of North Bay sent the following letter:
The North Bay board of trade strongly express the hope that the federal government in reconsidering the proposed tax upon gold production, will see that every consideration is given to the many small and low grade producers of gold in northern Ontario. Industrial and mercantile interests as well as the great body of men engaged in the industry of mining should be given consideration in such a manner that will tend to keep the wheels of progress in motion in this great area of mineral possibilities.
Representations have been made from all parts of the country, and I am pleased to note that the government reconsidered its blunder and has taken a wiser step. Even people far
74726-182^
away from the mining industry have made protests. Here is one:
The Minister of Mines in the Bennett government comes from Haileybury and his constituency embraces the rich Kirkland lake area, which mines about half of Ontario's annual gold production of $70,000,000.
If anyone in the government should know anything about the mining situation in Ontario, Mr. Gordon ought to be the one. But Mr. Gordon knew nothing whatever of the plan to put a ten per cent tax on gold until the day before Hon. E. N. Rhodes, Minister of Finance brought down the budget on Wednesday. Mr. Gordon was not even consulted and he happened to find out because the cabinet ministers were allowed a peek at the budget a few hours before it was delivered. In fact at Easter Mr. Gordon assured mining men there would be no tax levied on gold.
The question crops up: Why have a Minister of Mines, and why have a member from the mining district as minister? Mr. Gordon may have been proud of the post, but the present situation	makes	his	portfolio	look	like an
empty title and puts him in a foolish light.
I think the government realized its blunder when it received protests from all parts of the country interested, and as a result the Prime Minister last Thursday gave notice of the amendment to the gold tax proposal. The position of the Minister of Mines Was so ridiculous that it would have been only logical that he should have resigned his portfolio as Minister of Mines had there been no amendment	to	the gold	tax	proposal.But while the tax has been amended to the satisfaction of the Canadian people, I believe a discrimination still exists. Why discriminate against the mining industry when other industries make as big if not bigger profits? As has been well said this afternoon, there are big monopolies in this country in tobacco, in gasoline and other commodities, the profits of which	are as	big	as those	in the mining:industry,	if not	bigger. The	gold	tax does
discriminate against one particular industry, and the people of Canada I believe see the injustice of it on that ground.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) said that he would like to go a little further than placing a ten per cent tax on the gross production of gold; he wanted to nationalize the whole mining industry. Does he really want to kill the goose that lays the golden eggs? What we want is to regulate her diet, not to starve or kill her.
As to the other taxes proposed in this budget, they are of very little importance. The sugar tax has been reduced from two cents to one cent a pound, and. there is a reduction on beer, ale, porter, champagne and postal notes, from three cents to one cent, but these are of very little importance.
The Budget-Mr. Lucas

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that a time has come for a change in the fiscal policy of this country. I agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that we are passing through a period of great evolution, but it is not with the shibboleths, as he calls them, with which we have been supplied for the last four years, that we shall be able to cope with the situation. Let us be frank and honest. Let us rid ourselves of this narrow national and imperial protectionist policy. Let us have economic policies which will decentralize and thaw frozen capital, and bring about a better distribution of our production, that will relieve unemployment and bring back, if not prosperity, at least peace and contentment to the great mass of the people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members in this part of the house may I first be permitted to offer our sincere and deepest sympathy in the very sudden and great bereavement sustained by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes).
The budget, Mr. Speaker, as presented by the hon. Minister of Finance on April 18 last sets forth in very clear detail a financial picture of Canada. When one realizes the ever growing debt structure and increasing interest payments, not only is the picture not a pleasant one, but one wonders how long a population of ten million people can struggle along under such a burden.
The budget follows along the well beaten track of all budgets since confederation, and offers little hope to the struggling masses of any great measure of relief. As an orthodox budget there is very little to criticize, for the changes in taxation, while few and small in extent, are at least downwards, and likewise the tariff changes.
The reduction in the sugar tax to one cent a pound will no doubt be welcomed by the Canadian people and the substitution of a tax on gold to make up for the loss of revenue occasioned by the reduction in the sugar tax will on the whole be well received. The recent announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that adjustments are to be made in the gold tax as originally brought down so as to exempt the low grade mines from the operation of the tax should stop any controversy so far as they are concerned. The others in my opinion can well afford to pay, and I trust that the revenue to be derived from the industry will in no way be diminished by the change. It is the one industry that has prospered throughout the whole of this depression, first because of the fixed value of gold by law, and again by

its revaluation upwards by approximately seventy-five per cent. Also in my opinion the industry has paid less taxation in proportion to its means than any other industry, because it is allowed fifty per cent for depletion, and shareholders are allowed an exemption of fifty per cent on dividends for income tax purposes. But now that the government proposes to put a tax of ten per cent on the industry, its cry goes up to high heaven. Well, Mr. Speaker, my sympathies are all with those people who can ill afford to pay the sugar tax, and if the government had decided to wipe out the sugar tax entirely and make up that loss in revenue by an added tax on gold it would have received my support.
The Prime Minister a few days ago made the statement that generally speaking in the search for and mining of gold there was more money put into the ground than was taken out. If that is true, and I believe it is, we might have saved ourselves a great deal of energy and the hardship entailed in digging for this gold, and been just as well off in the end. In fact, we might have found ourselves in a much happier condition if we could have rid our minds of this gold superstition, and allowed our people to consume according to their ability to produce rather than have their consumption curtailed according to their ability to find gold, which is now no longer used in the everyday business of the country. It is generally recognized that superstition is the sign of ignorance, and that as education advances, superstition tends to disappear. Like the medicine men of Indian tribes who held their privileged position by cant and the fear which they instilled into the minds of the innocent members of their tribe, so the money changers of to-day hold their privileged position and power by the superstition and fear instilled into the minds of the people that unless their medium of exchange is based on gold they would all surely starve. It is an encouraging sign to note that there is a growing number of people throughout the world who at last are ridding their minds of such nonsense. Here might I be permitted to quote from a letter to the editor of the London Times by a body of business men in England asking for a parliamentary investigation into the workings of our money system: The modern paradox of poverty in the midst of plenty was the subject of a challenging passage in the speech of His Majesty the King at the opening of the world economic conference last year. His Majesty said:-
It cannot be beyond the power of man so to use the vast resources of the world as to ensure the material progress of civilization. No diminution in these resources has taken

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
place. On the contrary, discovery, invention, and organization have multiplied their possibilities to such an extent that abundance of production has itself created new problems.
Under modern scientifiie conditions the capacity of industry to produce is unlimited, and the continued existence of destitution, poverty, and unemployment throughout a large portion of the population demonstrates the fact that the present monetary system, the proper function of which is to facilitate the production of goods and their distribution to consumers as required, has broken down, both in its national and international aspects. The system is obsolete and has become a hindrance to the effective distribution of goods.
The object of production is consumption, and with approximately 90.000,000 people destitute or on the verge of destitution in the advanced nations which keep statistics, it cannot be suggested that the desire to consume is not present. Both these primary functions of the economic body-production and consumption- are frustrated, and' what should be a healthy and vigorous organism is paralyzed in peacetime by the failure of the monetary system of distribution.
The monetary system is man-made and can be altered; there is nothing sacrosanct about it.
We, the undersigned, in common with a large and rapidly growing body of citizens who are genuinely concerned at existing conditions, have come to the conclusion that gold is not essential as the basis for the issue of national money, and that nations should not be under obligation to make payments internationally with gold. A system must, in our view, be established under which the issue and recall of currency and credit will be regulated on a rational, national, and scientific basis, so that the correct number of money-tokens shall be available to consumers to enable them to enjoy the output of production.
We appeal, through your columns, for an immediate investigation by parliament of the fundamental principles which should govern our monetary system with a view to its reform in the interests of both producers and consumers.
There is, in our opinion, no need to wait for international agreement, since if Great Britain gives the lead, other countries will, we believe, find it in their own interests to follow.	.
This letter is signed by:
G. R. Clarke, Robert James, Maurice Jenks, Stanley Mackin, James Martin, A. G. Pape, Reginald Rowe, Semphill, A. Verdon-Roe, Vincent C. Vickers.
If any hon. member will take the trouble to look up the standing of those gentlemen he will find that they are all outstanding in the business life of Great Britain. I believe one of them was a former governor of the Bank of England.
The statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) at page 2270 of Hansard to the effect that the government proposes to bring down legislation to deal with farm debts will be well received by a great
many people throughout the country. He stated;
For certain individual debtors the burden has become unbearable and the government proposes to bring down at an early stage legislation designed to provide machinery whereby farmers who find themselves unable to pay the fixed charges on their outstanding debts will be able by an expeditious and inexpensive process to work out compromises with their creditors and to obtain new working capital. The guiding principle of this legislation will be to secure for the. farmer a simplified debt structure reduced in size to a point where the carrying charges will be within the capacity of the farm enterprise to pay.
That is all that is necessary to quote for my purpose. It sounds very good and I congratulate the government on their intention to introduce legislation along this muoh-needed line. I trust it will be as far-reaching in its powers as the marketing legislation now before the house. It is generally recognized that the farmers cannot pay their debt in full. If we are going to keep them on the. land and give them hope, some measure must be introduced to meet their conditions.
In his lengthy criticism of the budget, the financial critic of the official opposition, the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) certainly offered no hope to the people of Canada, should his party come into office, that they would leave the beaten track. I wish to congratulate him on the able manner in which he handled the subject, yet in my opinion his criticism was well described by an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen as negative criticism. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth ridiculed the Minister of Finance for not having left the beaten track, and he then quoted from a speech delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in a previous debate, as follows:
In this country, as in other countries, people have been staggering along under conditions that have been difficult, and have been clamouring for something out of the ordinary. Peoples all over the world have been very restive with governments because governments have been slow to depart from the beaten track.
May I pause here to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for having made that statement. It would appear that he at least has a grasp of present day conditions. Let me quote again the last part of this statement:
Peoples all over the world have been very restive with governments because governments have been slow to depart from the beatn track.
What has been the result of governments being slow to depart from the beaten track?
28S0

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
Look over the world to-day and what will you find? Democratic institutions which have been built up through the centuries are falling like tenpins, and why? In my opinion the Minister of Trade and Commerce placed his finger upon the very crux of the situation. People all over the world are not destroying democratic institutions just for the sake of setting up another form of government; they are doing it because these institutions have refused to leave the old beaten track and keep pace with the forward march pointed out by science and education. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth took about fifteen minutes of his two hour speech to criticize the budget because there were no signs that it was leaving the beaten track.
I agree with him in that criticism, but he harped so long upon that point that I think the house was led to believe that the Liberal party was going to offer something which would show that they were leaving the beaten track which has brought us to poverty and hardship and were going to blaze a new trail into the promised land. That would not have required much effort. The road would not need to be very long, because plenty is at our doorstep. However, apparently the wraiths and mists of Liberal principles [beclouded the vision of the hon. member, 'because after labouring for over two hours he found that the beaten track was worn so deep that he was not only unable to get out of it ;fout apparently was unable to see over the -sides what was going on about him; and we Iheard him shout from the depths the usual historic Liberal amendment. We in this corner of the house were disappointed in that amendment. Another hope was shattered. It was again the old story of the mountain labouring and bringing forth a mouse. The people of Canada now know what the Liberal party has to offer. Here is their amendment:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada s trade.
Not very much in that. Just regrets. It continues:
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment resigned to effect this end.
The first part of the amendment is a criticism of government policy which is not unexpected from the opposition. The second

part refers to some mysterious policies which are not disclosed. What are those policies? Time and again I have heard hon. members of the Liberal party state that what was needed to get back to normal was the Liberal policies of 1930. If my memory serves me aright, part of those policies referred to countervailing duties; in other words, a brick for brick policy-you put your tariff up and we will put ours up just as high; and every hon. member of the Liberal party voted for that policy. The Liberal tariff policy was in effect for nine years prior to 1930, but what happened? We lost completely our cattle market in the United States, and if any hon. member will look up Hansard of February 15, starting at page 542, he will see what the rest of the world was doing during those years. The rules of the house prevent me from quoting from any previous debate of this session but I would advise hon. gentlemen to look up Hansard and study those facts, which cannot very well be disputed. It will be found that while most of our exports enjoyed almost free entiy into world markets in 1922, by 1929 and the first part of 1930 almost prohibitive tariffs were imposed against us. I do not blame the Liberal party or its policies for what happened in the rest of the world, but I would point out what took place elsewhere when that party was in office. And I would ask them, if that happened under the old Liberal policy, what new policies do they propose to put into effect in order to induce the rest of the world to change its course? If they have any new policies, the people of the country should know what they are. During those years when they were in power Great Britain was still on a free trade basis, but free trade did not save Great Britain from the effects of the terrible depression. In fact, I think I am right in saying that unemployment was never so widespread there as during that period. Here in cold print is what we may expect, as set out in the last part of the amendment:
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect this end.
What does it mean? It means that until the Liberal party can change world tariffs and thus promote world trade it will be impossible to have improvement in Canada, or to apply successfully other policies respecting credit and employment. Is not that a rather hopeless picture? Unless the rest of the

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
world trades with us we are all to sit here and starve. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to subscribe to any such doctrine. Of course, it would be an ideal situation if we had a world brotherhood, but unfortunately we have not and so we 'must govern ourselves accordingly. In my opinion the quickest way to bring about world brotherhood is for Canada, for example, to assume national sovereignity over our medium of exchange and to detach herself from the control and domination of a world financial dictatorship, thus giving a lead to the rest of the world, showing them how to free themselves from the most insidious form of slavery that has ever existed in the history of the human race.
I wish to quote a few lines from a sermon delivered by the Very Rev. C. E. Riley, B.A., D.D., of Hamilton, Dean of Niagara. Speaking at the annual service of St. George's Society this year he said in part:
"I'm no economist, and God forbid that I should propose nonsense from this pulpit in the way of theories. Remember that you are but applying the palliative, but the cure is far more important. As members of an intelligent society, it is your duty to investigate the causes, to find something rotten in the state of Denmark. To find the dragon.
Why is there this poverty in the midst of plenty? Find the solution and solve it with your ballot.
Tell me why in a country, in a world of plenty, there is any need of starvation.
Is it honest to destroy goods? Is it right? Why?"
"It's a damned blasphemy and I use these words advisedly," stated Very Rev. C. E. Riley, B.A., D.D., Dean of Niagara, in a trenchant attack on the present system of distribution before a large congregation at the 92nd annual service of St. George's Society of Hamilton, at Christ Church Cathedral last night. The dean electrified a large congregation by his address and warned that if constitutional reforms were not put into effect, other means would be used.
Such a statement, coming from a high dignitary of the Anglican church, cannot be brushed aside with contempt, and therefore I appeal to hon. gentlemen to realize that we are sitting on a volcano that may erupt at any moment. We have already seen democratic institutions going down in many countries, and I make this prediction, that unless those that remain show by their action that they are capable of accommodating themselves to the new conditions, then it is only a matter of time until they all disappear. In other words, they must find the dragon and conquer him, and in my humble opinion that dragon is money power.
Let me say with all the emphasis at my command that I am opposed to high tariffs; but just as emphatically I say that in my
opinion these barriers cannot be removed until we first remove the cause. Listen to what Lloyd George, a staunch old Liberal, a real Liberal, has to say. Lloyd George is a Liberal who is living to-day, dealing with things as they are and not with conditions that existed in the dim and distant past. Speaking in a radio broadcast in Great Britain he said in part:
I do not propose to enter into the respective merits of free trade and protection. I am bound to accept the fact that we have become a highly protected country and that there is no prospect in the immediate future of persuading the nation to revert to free trade. I base my survey and suggestions on that assumption. These barriers undoubtedly aggravate some of the worst evils from which we are now suffering, but the causes of our economic troubles lie deeper. Whether under tariffs or under free trade plenty has produced universal poverty. The essential paradox of the world's economic trouble, including our own, is that under our existing economic system the exuberance of the earth's gifts has resulted in creating a famine in millions of households. The economic system under which we work has been shown up by the world crisis to be a pretentious fraud which has robbed humanity of its fair share of the good things which science has produced in abundance for the benefit of mankind.
I appeal to the Liberal party to wake up and realize that old shibboleths and party slogans will no longer satisfy a hungry and suffering humanity. The hopelessness of securing a world agreement was well exemplified at the world conference held in London last year. Repeated efforts were made to reach agreement, but without avail, and finally the representatives of the various nations were firmly convinced that the only thing left to do was to go home and put their own houses in order. Let us face the facts. If we cannot agree any better among ourselves than we exemplify in this house alone, how can we expect a conglomeration of peoples of the world, of different races and speaking various tongues, many of them filled with hatred and jealousies engendered through centuries of time, to meet and work out a satisfactory agreement?
The United Farmers of Alberta have been advocating for some time a system of planned economy. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Spealcman) on two occasions introduced in this house resolutions proposing that a council of social and economic research be set up to study such a plan. His resolution was finally adopted by the house. The very first plank of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation platform deals with planning and reads:
The establishment of a planned, socialized, economic order to make possible the most
The Budget-Mr. Lucas

efficient development of the national resources and the most equitable distribution of the national income.
If that plank of the platform is put into effect it means that a plan will be evolved for the development of the national resources and the equitable distribution of the national income. When such a plan is set up, will the nations of the world be allowed to dump their goods into this country and upset the plan? There would be little use in setting up a plan if it were to be knocked down so easily. As a matter of fact it is proposed, by even more effective methods than tariffs, namely, import and export boards and licences to regulate trade, and so we have a form of economic nationalism.
Let me quote from A. R. Orage, editor of the New English Weekly, his definition of economic nationalism. He said in part:
My own conception of economic nationalism can be defined as the coordination of the economic activities of a politically sovereign territory by a money system valid throughout the defined area, and designed for one purpose alone; that purpose being the increase of the prosperity of every member of the community, up to the point of utilizing, if required, the entire collective ability of the community to deliver goods and services.
That does not sound so terrible. Economic nationalism, as I understand it, will not prevent world trade but it first recognizes that the most important market is the home one and that our exports should consist only of the overspill after the home market has been fully supplied. Think what a market that would be if the people could only satisfy their wants from the abundance which surrounds them! What we want to do away with is the type of economic internationalism which we have to-day, which means the control of domestic economies by international money changers. This is the dragon we must destroy, and we must substitute for it an economic nationalism whereby the very lifeblood of the nation, finance, will be under the control of the nation for the welfare of the people. The mad rush for export markets is one of the greatest causes leading to war. Each country is short of home purchasing power, and so each one tries its best to get some from the other one. In reality, if the people of one country cannot buy their own goods which they have in abundance, how can they hope to buy from anyone else? If we had a proper money system which would enable the peoples of the world to make use of the abundance which surrounds them, world trade would then consist largely of countries exchanging fairly with one another their surpluses of domestic production for the surpluses of other countries

which produce those things which the former lack. We see the folly of present world trade, in Japan shipping textiles right into the British Isles, the mother of the textile trade. It is this fierce competition among the nations of the world to secure the others' purchasing power, without which to-day people cannot live, that sooner or later leads to war.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce in his very able speech pointed out the great changes which have been taking place in the past fifteen years. I would say that those changes have been in a developing process over many years, but they have become more noticeable in the past fifteen. Most of us can remember when a man learned a trade and then by his individual initiative produced something by his own efforts, thus making a living. That, as we all know, has largely changed; to-day a man makes little by his own efforts but produces mostly by association with his fellow man. A good example of this is the motor car industry. If you will take a trip through one of our large motor car factories you will see there thousands of men at work, each doing a special bit of werk toward making a car as it passes along a continuously moving platform. While each one contributes his bit in making the ear, not one of them is competent to make a car by himself, and so it is with most of our production to-day. The same thing is taking place on the farm. Under our power machine age man has become simply a cog in the wheel and every cog has to play its part to turn out the finished article. But science is developing that wheel to such an extent that it is getting along with fewer and fewer cogs and so we have more and more unemployment. By this cooperative effort between man and the power machine we have tremendously increased our productive capacity and have created an enormous pool of wealth but the trouble is that all are not able to draw from that pool equal to the amount they have contributed.
The pool is now so full it is running over and wasting. An example of this is the destruction of various commodities, and instead of using our brains and allowing this wealth to be used for what it was created, we are now planning every known device, for instance, by curtailment of production, to prevent goods from going into the pool. When amidst so much suffering of the people we see on the one hand destruction of commodities and the steps which are being taken to curtail production, and when on the other we are told that our only salvation is to work harder, which means greater production, and then to tighten our belts and be more thrifty, which

The Budget-Mr. Lucas
means less consumption, can one very much blame the people if they are losing faith in democratic institutions?
The amendment which was moved from this corner of the house is well worthy of consideration. It offers a way out; it is a departure from the beaten track, and I regret very much that it was declared out of order. But even that does not prevent it from expressing our viewpoint and I am convinced that the suggestions contained in that amendment will be widely endorsed by the thinking people of Canada.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, if we are to save civilization we must face the future with an entirely new outlook. Just as we discarded the ox cart for the motor car, so we must discard an outworn, privately owned money system, based on a condition of scarcity, for a national control of credit based on our ability to produce and the needs of the people. Major Douglas and Mr. MoGeer gave members of the banking committee somthing to think about by the evidence they gave before it recently and also by their public utterances, and while these two men differ somewhat in detail they are agreed on many points. Mr. McGeer showed commendable breadth of mind, when asked whether he understood Major Douglas' proposals, in saying that he understood them but that he saw difficulty in putting them into statutory form. He finished by saying:
Mind you, I do not want it to be taken from that, that I conclude that it cannot be done, because I have learned a long time ago that merely because I do not see a thing, that is not proof that it is not there.
Such an attitude is at least encouraging, but I am sorry to say that it appears to be in direct conflict with that evidenced by many members of this house. A 'lesson might well be taken from Japan, which has shown what may be accomplished when a people are prepared to face issues and to break with old traditions. When Japan decided to move forward not many years ago-that is, not many in the life of a nation'-she sent her experts on a tour of the world to learn what was being done. These experts found that Great Britain had the best navy, and so they decided to copy that, they found that France had the best and most efficient land army and so they decided to copy that, and so forth. Hon. members will agree that the advance made by the Japanese nation within a very short period from the inferior position which they occupied at that time to the rank of one of the first nations, is reckoned as one of the marvels of the world. Later on, when
the Japanese heard about the Douglas proposals they sent their experts to London to study them. They then invited Major Douglas to Japan, and instead of trying to belittle and to discredit his proposals, they sought to obtain all the information they could get, with the result that they have adapted at least part of his plan in using the national credit to subsidize the export of goods. And they have done this to such good purpose that last year they increased their export trade by fifty-three per cent.
While Major Douglas and Mr. McGeer both agree on national control and issue of credit, Mr. McGeer would have it distributed to the people as it is at present, that is through the old channels of production. Major Douglas differs; he points out that the amount of money so distributed through salaries, wages and dividends in a given period is never sufficient to purchase the total production, the result being our present situation. I was pleased to note that the Ottawa Journal, which always speaks with such assurance, endorses what Major Douglas has to say on this point. I quote in part from an editorial of April 2, 1934, entitled The Upturn in Wages, as follows:
The old cure for deflation was more deflation. People strangely had the notion that the way to cure a condition under which people weren't buying goods-a depression-was to make it harder for them to buy goods. To cut their wages.
Now there are conditions and cases where wage cuts are inescapable. Normally, however, as a general rule, wage cuts retard recovery, cannot do anything else. It is hard enough to work out a scheme of economics under which wages and salaries will always permit people to buy the whole of industrial and agricultural production; because the total of wages and salaries can never equal the total value of production. But what must be thought of the notion-all too common-that there can be anything like consumption of the total of production under low wages? The thing doesn't make sense.
So it is not only a question of raising wages, as the Journal points out. In my opinion President Roosevelt apparently has not yet grasped this point. He is issuing almost unlimited quantities of credit, but is using the old channels, overlooking the fact that until purchasing power is placed in the hands of the people no real prosperity is possible. In a speech recently made over the radio President Roosevelt stated that eighty-five per cent of the business of the United States is done by people receiving salaries of $2,000 a year or less. I think it is safe to say that one of our greatest difficulties to-day is due to the fact that a great majority of the people, who by
The Budget-Mr. Penas

their cooperative efforts have created such a vast pool of wealth that it is now running over, never have received sufficient purchasing power to enable them to buy back the goods they have produced. Major Douglas would remedy this by the issuance of social credit from the national pool direct to the people in order to make up this difference, and the evils of inflation would be overcome by the operation of the just price. Of course this would be a departure from the beaten track, but so is the marketing bill now before the house. Surely with the evils of the present system so painfully apparent it is not asking too much to say that we should give serious consideration to such proposals. At least that would show that we were doing our best to find a much needed solution of our problems.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first to extend my sympathy to hon. gentlemen opposite on the death of Mr. Lennox, whose sudden demise was very lamentable, as well as to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the sudden death of his wife.
The budget that was presented to this house on April 18, Mr. Speaker, is the fourth and perhaps the last of the present administration. Like those which preceded it, this budget contains a story of sadness, and seems to say, "He did the best he could with a bad job." The election of 1930 is not so distant that we cannot remember the attitude of the then opposition with respect to the administration then in power. The oncoming crisis was not at that time a world crisis, according to hon. gentlemen opposite; crises were not possible under good government, they said. "Put us into power and there will be no crisis," they said. Well, those who followed their advice and voted in that way have deeply regretted their action in the last four years. The crisis hit Canada hard and is still hitting it. The old Canadian ship of state is riding a rough sea; its crew are none too confident of weathering the storm and the captain is none too sure of reaching a certain port.
I listened with great interest to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance; I have read and re-read that speech, and it seems like going over the inventory of a bankrupt concern which, under good management, once was a thriving industry. The administration of to-day, in common with other Conservative administrations, has not been very fortunate in the way of raising revenues but has proved very successful in raising taxes. So, as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) pointed out, this year all taxes have been maintained with the exception of the

sugar tax, which has been cut in half. We need not be grateful for the fact that no new taxes have been imposed, because it is not due to generosity. If we have no new taxes it is because we are no longer taxable, or rather because we could be taxed but the tax could not be collected, since we are unable to pay it. During the last fiscal year we collected less taxes than were collected in the previous year, but let no one be led into error by that fact. In 1929-30 we collected in taxes $378,551,000; in 1930-31 that dropped to $296,276,000, and in 1932-33 it dropped still further to $275,054,000. In connection with customs and excise duties and war tax revenues it is interesting to note the fluctuations of the sales tax, which in 1929-30 produced roughly $44,000,000. In 1930-31 we reduced that to $20000,000, but when the present administration came into office the sales tax was increased to six per cent, so that in 1931-32 it produced about $41,000,000 and in 1932-33 about $56,000,000. Under the Libera;! regime we reduced the sales tax and produced surpluses, because our international and external trade was flourishing for the reason that our fiscal policies were directed towards free and expanding trade.
I should like to quote some figures to indicate how our debt has continually increased since this government came into office. In round figures our debt has increased as follows:

When the present administration took office they scrambled their fiscal policy and for that reason had to pile on the sales tax. For the same reason our revenues have gone down. Of course when we say that, immediately the objection is thrown out that the country is facing a general crisis. Let us admit that. But we were told that no crisis can exist under good government. We said there was a coming crisis in 1929 and 1930. We were preparing for it; we were trying to enlarge our markets, we were endeavouring to expand trade, but we were told it was foolish.
Well, in 1933, Great Britain imported 1,300,000 hundredweight less wheat from Canada than in 1932, but got 2,500,000 hundredweight more from Russia than she did the year before, 4,000,000 hundredweight more from the Argentine, and 5,000,000 hundredweight more from Australia. In 1933 Great Britain bought 1,200,000 hundredweight more barley from Russia than in 1932; 3,000,000 hundredweight

The Budget-Mr. Penas
more from Roumania; 2,500,000 hundredweight more from the United States, but she bought 2,000,000 hundredweight less from Canada. In 1933 Great Britain bought 600,000 hundredweight more oats from Russia than she did in the year before, 220,000 hundredweight more from Germany, but a million hundredweight less from Canada. She bought 324,000 hundredweight more of bacon from Canada than she did in the year before. So that taken all in all, our trade may be said to be on the hog.
Let me now place on Hansard some figures showing our revenue. The following table will serve to illustrate the situation:

These figures indicate a steady decrease year by year instead of the benefits which have been so loudly proclaimed, and which it was said we would derive from blasting our way into the markets of the world.
I can readily imagine the feelings of the Minister of Finance when at page 2283 of Hansard he had to admit that the debt had increased, as I have already said, by some $135,000,000. And I can quite readily understand his situation when he had to admit, as it is reported on the same page of Hansard, that the deficit on ordinary account would be $24,000,000. Again I can imagine his state of mind when, as appears at page 2275 of Hansard, he stated that the failure to reach the estimated revenue by some $33,000,000 has naturally been disappointing. Indeed, it is sad, but we have been accustomed to very little else. The British budget is being called the sunshine budget. We have had Robb and Dunning budgets which indicated prosperity. Then, we have had Rhodes budgets, but none of these roads has yet led us out of misery.
The situation becomes more distressing, and we find that we are still voting in blank millions upon millions for relief purposes. We had been told that unemployment would be stopped at once. It is still rampant, and the sums we spend are appalling. I do not think that the Canadian people really know the amounts being spent for relief, and they do not realize that those sums must all come from them. We are sort of robbing Peter to pay Paul, but this cannot be carried on much longer. Some proportionate return should result from the money spent on relief. We cannot continue spending at that rate. We are heaping millions upon millions of dollars upon the large industrial centres and other portions of western Canada, but what has
been done to help agriculturists in other parts of Canada out of their troubles? The minister said that the expenditures made since 1930 by the dominion for unemployment relief have reached a total of $115,500,000, to which may be added the cost of the wheat bonus in 1931, amounting to $12,700,000, and $2,400,000 advanced for employment in railway shops, making a total of $130,600,000, The expenditure for relief in the year 1933-34 is estimated at $36,000,000. These figures are staggering when we realize the very little that is being done for the eastern farmers.
It is my privilege to represent in this honourable house a constituency which is largely rural. In the few urban sections of that county relief has 'been given out, but in other sections of it conditions are deplorable. Farm products have been at bottom prices for the last two years, and there are no immediate signs of betterment. Many farms have been let go. The index price of farm products in 1930 averaged 82-3. In December of this year it was 53-3, indicating a fall of 46 per cent.
Let us now consider the pulp industry. In 1932 we produced $57,943,419 worth less pulp and $71,751,802 worth less paper products than we produced in 1930. In my constituency that was a fearful blow to a large percentage of the population. As I have said, there are some centres in which the whole population is engaged in farming, but there are many villages and rural communities in my constituency where people are working either as daily manual labourers or as jobbers. These people, and they are quite numerous, depended for their existence for years upon the wood and pulp industry, and for the last three years most of them have been on the verge of starvation.
These trade agreements, and the new market openings which were promised, did not help us much. In 1933 we exported of paper and manufactures of paper $66,134,111 worth less than in 1930, and $15,705,342 less of pulp; $5,130,401 less of cheese, $416,369 less of butter, $18,523,737 less of wheat flour, $63,373,340 less of wheat, $5,504,758 less of potatoes, $672,534 less of dressed beef; and I could quote many other similar figures.
Let me point out that the price' of bacon and hams in 1930 was $24 per hundredweight, and only $11 in 1933. The price of butter was 30 cents per pound in 1930 and only 17 cents in 1933.
